title: FlashWAF: a page-mapped flash simulator
description:
FlashWAF is an open-source Python simulator that models page-mapped Flash Translation Layer (FTL) address mapping, out-of-place page updates, greedy garbage collection, and page-program write amplification under controlled synthetic workloads.

Designed for storage systems research and pedagogy, FlashWAF isolates algorithmic FTL dynamics in a pure-Python, dependency-light framework. It includes reproducible benchmark pipelines, raw trial outputs, automated invariant tests, and analysis scripts.

Core Modeling Components

  • Page-Mapped FTL: Dynamic logical-to-physical (L2P) address translation table.
  • Out-of-Place Updates: Tri-state page lifecycles (FREE → VALID → INVALID) with invalidation counters upon host overwrites.
  • Greedy Garbage Collection: Victim block selection maximizing invalid page count, live valid-page copying, and block-level erasures with erase-count tie-breaking.
  • Write Amplification Factor (WAF): Exact measurement of total flash page programs per user page request: WAF = (Host Page Writes + GC Copy Writes) / Host Page Writes.
  • Synthetic Workloads: Uniform random, parameterized hot/cold (e.g. 80/10, 90/5), and discrete Zipfian distributions using reproducible common random numbers.

Included Experimental Benchmarks

  • Primary 30-Seed Paired Experiment: Prepopulated active LBAs across 40%, 70%, and 85% mapped occupancy under uniform vs. 80/10 hot/cold traffic (180 condition runs total). Measured paired hot/cold-minus-uniform contrasts: +0.32987 at 40% occupancy (95% CI [0.32665, 0.33310]), +0.60656 at 70% ([0.60054, 0.61258]), and +0.80465 at 85% ([0.78676, 0.82253]).
  • Robustness & Sensitivity Grid: Evaluates warm-up lengths (0 to 10,000 updates), geometry scaling (16x32 vs 32x32 blocks), and workload skew variations at 70% occupancy across 10 paired seeds.

Scientific Scope & Boundaries

FlashWAF is a discrete computational research model, not an empirical emulator of physical NAND hardware. It does not model physical NAND analog timing (program/erase latencies), multi-channel parallelism, wear leveling pools, crash recovery journals, or hardware bit-error ECC. Findings characterize this simulator under synthetic workloads and do not predict physical SSD endurance.
